To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the activity of neurons in the NCl of pigeons is similar to the activity in PFC neurons of humans and other mammals and is related to the successful retention of information in working memory.

the neostiatrum caudolaterle of pigeons contains a population of neurons that show activity changes during a working memory task that are similar to those observed for working memory neurons in the prefrontal cortices of mammals.
working memory neurons are present in the NCL, a brain structure of the avian pallium that is homologous to the mammalian PFC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neuronal basis of executive control functions, such as attention, working memory, and response inhibition in pigeons.
the neuronal basis of working memory in the neostriatal system of pigeons.
the neuronal basis of cognitive processes, in particular working memory and executive control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural mechanisms underlying working memory in birds and mammals are similar, but not the same.
the neuronal mechanisms underlying working memory are highly similar in pigeons and primates, despite the fact that they are based on a completely different brain structure.
the neuronal basis of working memory is not confined to the neocortex but can be found in the NCL.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
birds have a cognitive capacity similar to that of mammals.
the neuronal substrate for working memory is not a neocortical invention but a more ancient evolutionary achievement.
the NCL in birds, as the PFC in mammals, provides the neuronal substrate for the cognitive functions of working memory and response inhibition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of the neocortex in mammals did not result in a new type of information processing, but in a new type and arrangement of the neuronal substrate for the same cognitive processes.
the evolution of the cognitive abilities of birds and mammals is not only driven by differences in brain size, but also by the functional properties of the neuronal substrate.
the neural mechanisms underlying working memory are highly conserved across species.
